summary: Describes methods and scenarios for deploying IPv6 alongside existing IPv4 services in broadband provider networks, covering cable, Ethernet, DSL and wireless LAN access technologies. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: Internet providers have to add the new kind of address while keeping the old one working. This note walks through ways to do that for cable, DSL and other home connections.

subtitle: Deploying IPv6 in cable, DSL, Ethernet, wireless, and power-line broadband networks.

tldr.problem: Internet service providers running broadband networks must transition from IPv4 to IPv6 while maintaining existing services. Different broadband access technologies (cable, DSL, Ethernet, wireless, power-line) have different constraints and require different IPv6 deployment strategies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes deployment scenarios for each broadband technology, covering tunneling-based approaches (for IPv6-over-IPv4) and native IPv6 deployments. It addresses addressing, routing, multicast, QoS, security, and network management for each technology. Three approaches are outlined: tunneling (least change), native IPv6 (most change), and MPLS 6PE (middle ground) for core networks.
tldr.outcome: This informational guide helped early IPv6 deployments but the landscape has evolved. Today, most networks support native IPv6 as well as dual-stack IPv4/IPv6. DHCPv6 and stateless address auto-configuration have become standard. Tunneling is now used mainly for edge cases rather than mainstream deployment.

facts.label: Broadband technologies covered
facts.value: Cable/HFC, DSL, Ethernet, Wireless LAN, Power-line

today: RFC 4779 is an Informational document and has not been updated or obsoleted. It provided crucial guidance for early IPv6 deployments in the mid-2000s. Today, the landscape has evolved: most broadband networks support native dual-stack IPv4/IPv6, DHCPv6 and stateless address auto-configuration are widely deployed, and tunneling is rarely used for mainstream access networks. However, the document's framework remains relevant for understanding how different broadband technologies handle IPv6, and organizations still deploy using models described here. Newer work (like RFC 4029) expanded on these deployment scenarios.

sections.title: IPv6 Deployment in Broadband Networks
sections.content: RFC 4779 provides a detailed analysis of how to deploy IPv6 in broadband access networks while maintaining coexistence with existing IPv4 services. The document covers five major broadband technologies: Cable/HFC (Hybrid Fiber Coax), Broadband Ethernet, xDSL (Digital Subscriber Line), Wireless LAN, and emerging Broadband Power Line Communications (PLC/BPL). It discusses how each technology must be upgraded to support IPv6, addresses the key infrastructure components, and describes deployment models ranging from tunneling-based approaches (minimal infrastructure change) to native IPv6 (full dual-stack support). The goal is to guide Internet Service Providers (ISPs) and Network Access Providers in planning and executing IPv6 deployment according to their network architecture and business needs.
sections.eli5: This document is a guidebook for Internet providers who want to add IPv6 to their networks. It covers five types of home Internet (cable, phone lines, fiber, wireless, and power lines) and explains what needs to change for each type.

sections.title: IPv6 Deployment Approaches and Cable Networks
sections.content: The RFC describes three core approaches for deploying IPv6. Tunneling has minimal impact on the access provider network; IPv6 traffic is encapsulated in IPv4 packets and transported across an IPv4 core to the service provider edge. Native IPv6 deployment upgrades access routers to dual-stack, enables an IPv6 Interior Gateway Protocol (OSPFv3 or IS-IS), and routes native IPv6 traffic. MPLS 6PE is a middle ground approach where only edge routers need full IPv6 support. For cable networks specifically using the DOCSIS standard, the RFC primarily describes tunneling-based IPv6 deployment since DOCSIS 2.0 lacks native IPv6 support. Multiple scenarios are presented: (1) Host directly tunnels to ER, (2) GWR at customer site tunnels to ER, (3) Dual-stack CMTS acting as ER with native IPv6. Challenges include lack of IPv6 support in DOCSIS, IPv6 Neighbor Discovery limitations, IPv6 traffic classification, and multicast handling. IPv6 addresses can be assigned statically, via DHCPv6, or through stateless auto-configuration.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to add IPv6: hide it in IPv4 packets, upgrade all routers, or use a special MPLS trick. Cable networks currently need to wrap IPv6 inside IPv4 unless they upgrade to newer equipment that supports native IPv6.

sections.title: IPv6 in DSL, Ethernet, and Wireless Networks
sections.content: DSL and Broadband Ethernet networks support native IPv6 more readily. Both use similar deployment models: Point-to-Point (dedicated customer links), PPP Terminated Aggregation (PTA, with customers aggregated at a BRAS), L2TPv2 Access Aggregation (LAA, tunneling customer traffic), and Hybrid (IPv4 and IPv6 in parallel). IPv6 addressing can use stateless auto-configuration, DHCPv6, or DHCP Prefix Delegation (DHCP-PD) to distribute /48 prefixes to customer sites. Both support IPv6 multicast with ASM (Any-Source Multicast) and SSM (Source-Specific Multicast) models. Wireless LAN (WLAN) broadband deployments are described with three scenarios based on whether the network access point (NAP) handles Layer 2 or Layer 3 termination. IPv6 QoS in wireless networks must account for radio spectrum constraints using IPv6 classifiers for traffic differentiation. Security considerations include privacy extensions for stateless auto-configuration and protection against IPv6-specific attacks. The emerging Broadband Power Line Communications (BPL/PLC) technology requires similar infrastructure upgrades to support IPv6 addressing, routing, multicast, QoS, and security.
sections.eli5: Phone-line and fiber internet can more easily upgrade to native IPv6. WiFi and power-line internet also need upgrades but can support IPv6 with the right equipment and techniques.

sections.title: Address Assignment, Routing, and Security
sections.content: Across all broadband technologies, the RFC discusses multiple address assignment approaches. Stateless auto-configuration allows devices to self-configure from router advertisements (RA messages) without server interaction. DHCPv6 allows dynamic assignment of individual addresses from a pool. DHCP Prefix Delegation (DHCP-PD) allows the provider to delegate address blocks (typically /48 prefixes) to customer premises equipment, which then subdivide the block for local networks. For routing, the document describes static routing, RIPng, and OSPFv3. Customers typically use default routes pointing to the provider's edge router. IPv6 multicast requires MLD (Multicast Listener Discovery) snooping on Layer 2 devices. QoS mechanisms should mirror IPv4 approaches, using traffic classifiers based on IPv6 headers. Security considerations include enabling IPv6 privacy extensions, firewall filtering at edge routers, unicast reverse path forwarding (uRPF), access control lists (ACLs) on provider-facing interfaces, and protection against floods of IPv6 control traffic. The RFC emphasizes that IPv6 security should be as strong as IPv4 security but tailored to IPv6-specific features.
sections.eli5: Providers assign addresses automatically, via DHCP, or by giving customer routers a block to divide up locally. For routing and security, they use similar techniques as IPv4 but adapted for IPv6.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations and Impact
sections.content: The RFC emphasizes that the addressing rules represent examples that follow current regional registry assignment policies but can be adapted to ISP business needs. The scope is to advise on upgrading existing infrastructure to support IPv6 services. An RFC recommendation to upgrade a device to dual-stack does not stop an SP from adding a new device to its network to perform necessary IPv6 functions. The costs involved with such an approach can be offset by lower impact on existing IPv4 services. For cable networks, using IPv6 for management purposes in the control plane is identified as a good initial step before deploying IPv6 for customer data plane services. This allows ISPs to overcome IPv4 address space constraints in management networks while keeping minimal operational impact. The document provides detailed scenarios for each broadband technology to guide practical deployment decisions.
sections.eli5: Different providers can adapt the techniques to fit their business needs and financial constraints. Starting with using IPv6 for managing equipment (not customer data) is a low-risk first step for cable networks.
